thread.title: I've decided to sell Kroger ( KR ). This is the first sale i

author: David Harper, CFA
title: I've decided to sell Kroger ( KR ). This is the first sale i
text:
I've decided to sell Kroger ( KR ). This is the first sale in my public equities portfolio (full portfolio at bottom). I only bought KR according to the anti-Amazon thesis (articulated nicely by Eric Parnell here ); on October 17th, I perceived a discount of at least 25%, and since then, 31% price appreciation has been achieved. As a value investor - which signifies for me that I perceive a medium- to long-term fair price (or equity capitalization level) that is above the current price, with reasonable safety - I simply no longer have my reason for owning. I follow public equity markets only a few hours a week; this limits the number of positions I can hold. What doesn't show up in my spreadsheet yet is the "mental maintenance factor" of each stock. I think I will call this bugbear factor: how much worry time does it occupy in my brain. On the best-end of the range are Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Bank of America (NYSE: BAC ), which have required very little attention from me, in general, because I bought them with huge margins of safety. On the other hand, I realized that I have to think too much about three of my holdings: Cloudera (NYSE: CLDR ), Discovery Communications (NASDAQ: DISCK ), and KR. And, to a lesser extent, CVS Health (NYSE: CVS ).
I am not bigly negative on KR. Rather, I just do not want to monitor this huge business with its headwinds in light of what looks like moderate long-term upside at best and amounts to broad low-beta (i.e., 0.43) consumer-defensive exposure. What inspires me about KR includes (on the positive side of the aisle, pun intended):
The Restock Kroger initiative is smart. Um, on paper. It aspires to apply data science to the business, and management looks to be committed with big investments. But this is a show-me situation. I can't speak for you, but I'm a long way from associating Kroger with its cool plan to "build [their] Internet of Things sensor network, video analytics and machine learning networks and complement those innovations with robotics and artificial intelligence to transform the customer experience." It looks to have gone from clearly undervalued to perhaps slightly undervalued (but I do not think by much; the highest analyst price target is $34.00. I think smart money should sell if it goes above $30.00). You've now got an attractive forward P/E of about 14.0, but same-store sales growth could be at low as 1.1% (seems to be the implication on the last call). Maybe the best argument here is its trailing ROIC of 12.31%. It is paying a 1.74% dividend, and it has a 3-year growth rate of 13.5%. Here in Southern California, Ralphs supermarket is much superior to Vons in my experience as a weekly shopper. Anecdotal experience is not enough.
